Yes, they're two separate fields on the same `GitSource` model (`server/internal/model/model.go:518` and `:546`). Which one a source fills in depends on what kind of source it is.

- **`url`**: a remote source. You named a repository URL (`-C https://…` or `-C OWNER/REPO`), and that URL is what the code is fetched from. There's no `localDirectory`. This is what 5wr1 has.
- **`upstreamUrl`**: a local source. It always comes with `localDirectory`, and the code comes from your checkout on disk. `upstreamUrl` is just the remote your client reported for that checkout: the remote the checked-out branch tracks, else `origin`, else its only remote. That's why krpfz shows `git@github.com:ibuildthecloud/discobox.git`, because your `disco2` main tracks that remote. It's metadata about the checkout, not where the code was fetched from.

They end up in similar places downstream:

- **Remote in the box:** for a cache-delivered source, whichever URL applies becomes the sandbox's `origin`. Older (non-cache) local deliveries added `upstreamUrl` as a remote named `upstream` instead.
- **Pool cache:** `cacheKey` is derived from that URL, so the two boxes' primaries landed in different pool caches (`ibuildthecloud/discobox` vs `discobox-ai/discobox`).
- **Which repository a box counts as:** `GitSource.RepositoryURL()` (`model.go:597`) uses `url` if it's set and falls back to `upstreamUrl`. Approval-rule repository matching and the judge both go through it.
- **Listing and grouping:** `GitSource.Root()` doesn't use either URL for a local source; it keys on `localDirectory`.

In practice, a policy or approval rule written for `github.com/discobox-ai/discobox` matches 5wr1. Whether it also matches krpfz depends on how the comparison normalizes the two URLs (SSH vs HTTPS, the `.git` suffix), and I didn't check that. Either way it can't match krpfz's primary, which is your fork: `ibuildthecloud/discobox` is a different repository.

result.output:
## Source delivery

Each materialized source also receives an opaque source-data key before the
provider boundary. It is the origin-key derivation (`originkey.Of`) applied to
the client host ID and that source's normalized `GitSource.Root()`, which makes
the primary source's key the sandbox's origin key (`model.SandboxOriginKey`,
ADR 0111); source-code references get independent identities from their own
roots. An
incomplete host/source identity opts out rather than sharing under an ambiguous
key. The pool runtime uses the key only to select durable pool-local storage and
exposes that storage inside a sandbox by source slug; no control-plane or
runtime component interprets its contents. The keys are folded into the
create's spec fingerprint (`sourceDataFingerprint`), so a container built
without those mounts is rebuilt.

Every Git source of a sandbox is delivered by a client into its pool's cache of
Git, and nothing chooses between deliveries
([ADR 26-10-10-545](../../../../docs/adr/26-10-10-545-git-reaches-a-pool-only-from-a-client-and-is-cached-there-per-remote.md)
§1). `resolveSourceDelivery` records that on each source at create — the
primary `Source` and every `SourceCodeReferences` entry alike — as
`GitSource.Delivery = cache` and a `GitSource.CacheKey`. Both are the server's
record: a create that names a delivery is refused, and a cache key a client
sent is replaced. The server never runs Git and the pool never fetches from a
remote.

`sourceCacheKey` names the pool cache, through `sourcecache`:

| The source | The key |
| --- | --- |
| Has a remote | `remote/<host>/<path>`: the remote, normalized (`sourceref.NormalizeRemote`) |
| Has none, and its client reported a host identity | `directory/<sourceDataKey>` |
| Neither | `sandbox/<sandboxID>/<slug>`: a cache of its own, removed with the sandbox |

- A remote-URL source's remote is its `URL`; a local checkout's is the
  `UpstreamURL` its client reported (`sourceRemote`). A value that is not a
  network remote — a path, `file://`, a pool's origins host — is no remote.
- The host identity is deliberately not part of a remote's key: every member of
  a project shares one cache per remote on a pool (§2).
- A sandbox creating a discobox is treated the same. Its origin and its remote
  are its own claim, and that is harmless: the pool holds a sandbox to what it
  sends and what its own namespaces reach, whichever cache it names (§7).

`GitSource.NoLocalRepository`, `NoLocalCommits` and `NoLocalGitDirectory` are
still recorded facts about the client's filesystem, and decide nothing here.
Only `NoLocalRepository` matters later: its commits are gone once that create
is over, so a client cannot deliver it again
([ADR 0045](../../../../docs/adr/0045-a-directory-with-no-repository-is-delivered-by-push.md)).

Sandboxes created earlier keep their recorded delivery, and it keeps its
meaning: `push` is a bare repository the pool made for that sandbox, which a
client pushes into; `clone` is a source the sandbox fetched itself. Nothing
rewrites them (§8).

`clientDeliveredSources` is what a sandbox waits on: every `cache` and `push`
source, and — only while the sandbox has never run (`sandboxHasNeverRun`) — a
local source recorded as `clone`. That last one was served live from the
developer's Git directory, which no pool does now, so one that has not cloned
yet has nothing to clone until a client pushes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant P as Pool agent
    C->>S: create (origin, checkout.commit)
    S->>S: delivery = cache, cacheKey
    S-->>C: sandbox
    par delivery
        loop every client-delivered source
            C->>S: pin (refs and the object each names)
            S->>P: proxied pin, naming the cache
            opt the cache lacks something
                C->>S: git push --atomic (branch, snapshot, remote's refs)
                S->>P: proxied git-receive-pack
            end
        end
        C->>S: complete-source-push (confirms every source's commit)
    and provisioning
        S->>P: create
        opt no delivery reported yet
            S->>S: state = awaiting_source
        end
    end
    S->>P: create again → namespace HEAD → sandbox clones → settle
    P->>P: start harness
```

A delivery does not wait for the sandbox (§3). Its route names the sandbox and
the slug, the proxy names the cache, and the pool needs nothing else, so the
client delivers while the image is pulled. `CompleteSandboxSourcePush` is
therefore accepted for any sandbox still owed its source that has never run —
`pending` as well as `awaiting_source` — and a sandbox whose delivery is
reported before it is provisioned never parks. Any other state is refused: a
completion there would restart a sandbox out from under whatever runs in it.

The push transport is the sandbox Git proxy
(`internal/server/sandbox_git_proxy.go` → `pool-agent/githttp`); delivery adds
no transport of its own. Each source has its own origin there, addressed by
its slug: a namespace of a cache, or a repository of its own.
The commit is fixed at create in `Checkout.Commit`; `complete-source-push` only
confirms it, and a mismatch is refused.

Completion is one report for the whole sandbox, not one per source: the client
delivers every client-delivered source and then names them all, keyed by slug, in a

Yes. Every source a sandbox gets today is delivered by the client pushing it, and neither the server nor the pool agent ever fetches from GitHub. This is ADR `26-10-10-545` ("Git reaches a pool only from a client and is cached there per remote"). The sandboxes DESIGN.md says it plainly: "The server never runs Git and the pool never fetches from a remote." Every source created now is recorded as `delivery: cache`, which matches both of your boxes, and a create request that names a delivery itself is refused.

**How a remote-URL source like 5wr1 gets there** (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/cachedeliver.go:194`, `deliverRemote`): your CLI does the remote work itself.
1. It runs `git ls-remote` against the URL to learn the refs, which transfers no objects.
2. It asks the pool, through the server, which of those refs it can "pin", meaning create from objects already in its cache. If the pool has everything, nothing more happens.
3. Otherwise the CLI fetches into its own cache at `~/.cache/discobox/client/git/<remote>`: first what the pool already has, then the remote, so each leg carries only what's missing.
4. It pushes to the server, which proxies the `git-receive-pack` to the pool agent (`sandbox_git_proxy.go` → `pool-agent/githttp`). Then it sends `complete-source-push`.

The code comments call out the cost: the first create for a remote that neither your client nor the pool has seen moves the history twice, remote → client → pool. They say that's the price of a pool that never fetches and never holds a credential, paid once per remote per pool.

**A local source like krpfz** works the same way, except it pushes from your working repo instead of a client cache.

**The only "pull"** is inside the pool: the sandbox clones its workspace from the pool's cache namespace. That stays on the pool and never goes out to the network.

**Two caveats:**
- **Older sandboxes:** `clone` is still a valid recorded value, and it meant the sandbox fetched the source itself, from `url` or from your `localDirectory` through the pool. `push` meant a bare repo the pool made for that one sandbox. Sandboxes created before the ADR keep those values, but new creates never get them.
- **Inside the box:** `origin` in the sandbox is set to the real remote (`url` or `upstreamUrl`). So the harness itself can `git fetch` or `git push` to GitHub later, through the pool proxy, if it has a credential. That's the agent's own traffic, not source delivery by the server or pool.
Does code for other delivery modes exist today?

## Context

A source reaches a sandbox three ways today, chosen by `sourceNeedsPush`:

| Source | Delivery | The sandbox clones from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remote URL | clone | the remote itself, through the pool proxy |
| Local, client and server on one host | clone | the pool, serving the developer's live Git directory |
| Local, anything else | push | the pool, serving a bare repository made for that sandbox |

Issue #139 measured what that costs. A remote-URL source is a full-history
clone over the WAN, made by every sandbox, after it boots: 16–47s for a
27.6 MiB repository, set by the remote's speed at that moment. A pushed source
moves the same full history into an empty repository on every create. Nothing
a pool has received is reused by the next sandbox.

Three further problems share that cause:

- **A private remote has no delivery.** ADR 0128 proposed lending the user's
  credential to the pool for one fetch. It puts a user credential on the
  control plane and the pool, and it was not built.
- **The same request behaves differently by where the server runs.** The live
  origin exists only for a co-located client, behind a host-identity comparison
  and a provider's local source roots, and it is a second way of serving an
  origin (`live-origins.json`, the snapshot in `pool-agent/githttp`) with its
  own failure, a race with the developer's `git gc`.
- **The sandbox's remotes describe the plumbing.** `origin` is the pool and the
  real remote is `upstream`, so an agent's `git push origin` and every tool
  that reads `origin` point at the wrong place.

## Alternatives rejected

- **The pool fetches with a credential the client lends (ADR 0128).** The data
  moves once, which is its whole advantage. A user's credential transits the
  server and the pool, and a create becomes a credential-bearing request.
- **The pool fetches anonymously when the remote is public.** No credential is
  involved, but it is a second delivery chosen by probing a remote, and the
  pool is back to depending on a remote's speed and reachability.
- **The pool fetches through the client, which adds the credential.** It needs
  a channel from a pool to one particular client — what 0128 rejected a
  credential callback for — and the bytes still cross the client's link.
- **A cache per user.** It needs no trust between project members. It also
  gives no reuse between them, which is where a team's reuse is.
- **One repository per sandbox borrowing objects through `alternates`.** 0058
  §4 rejected alternates because a repack on either side breaks the chain. A
  namespace is one repository with one object store, and has no chain.
- **A shallow or partial clone in the sandbox.** `--depth` takes away the
  history an agent reads. `--filter=blob:none` fetches blobs from the remote
  for the life of the sandbox, on demand, with a credential it may not have.
- **Keeping the live origin for a co-located client.** It saves one local
  push. It keeps the host comparison, the provider's source roots and a second
  origin implementation, and it keeps a local server behaving unlike a remote
  one.
- **Reading a declared-sources file through `git archive --remote` or a
  host's file API.** GitHub answers the first with an error over HTTPS, and
  the second is one integration per host with its own credential.
- **Caching Git in the pool proxy.** A fetch is a negotiated `POST`; no two
  are the same request.

# 0128 — A private remote source is fetched with a credential the client lends

- **Status**: Rejected by [26-10-10-545](26-10-10-545-git-reaches-a-pool-only-from-a-client-and-is-cached-there-per-remote.md), which delivers a private remote from the client and never lends the pool a credential

  [0031](0031-agent-credentials-are-a-portable-protocol-with-ephemeral-sentinels.md),
  [0045](0045-a-directory-with-no-repository-is-delivered-by-push.md),
  [0055](0055-a-delivered-source-settles-before-its-sandbox-runs.md),
  [0058](0058-a-push-delivered-source-has-a-pool-side-origin.md), and
  [0126](0126-a-sandbox-does-not-share-a-host-or-a-filesystem-with-its-pool.md).

## Context

`-C` takes a repository URL, and now GitHub shorthand for one (`owner/repo`,
`github.com/owner/repo` → `https://github.com/owner/repo.git`). A remote source
is delivered by clone: `sourceNeedsPush` returns false for any source without a
`LocalDirectory`, and pool-agent's `materializeGitSource` clones the URL
directly (`gitSourceCloneURL`).

That clone runs with no credential. Pool agents are given none, deliberately:
a credential on the pool host outlives the create that needed it, is shared by
every sandbox on the pool, and belongs to a user the pool does not represent.
So a private repository fails, and it fails late. The client's own `git
ls-remote` (`resolveRemoteGitRef`) succeeds with the user's credentials, the
create is accepted, and the clone fails in the pool agent, in a reconcile loop
nobody is watching.

The model we want is `docker pull`'s: the credential stays with the client and
is lent for one operation. Two pieces are already in place:

- **A parked delivery phase.** A push-delivered source parks its sandbox in
  `awaiting_source` until the client completes it (ADR 0045, ADR 0055), so the
  client is known to be present at create and nothing runs before the source
  settles.
- **A pool-side origin.** Every push-delivered source has a bare repository on
  the pool host that the worktree is cloned from and that the sandbox's `origin`
  points at (ADR 0058). Remote sandboxes clone from the same place (ADR 0126
  §4).

What is missing is a way to fill that origin from a URL the pool can reach but
not read.

## Decision

### 1. The client reports whether the URL reads anonymously; the server decides

Before create, the client runs `git ls-remote` against a remote source twice as
needed: first anonymously (no credential helper, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`), then
with its normal configuration. A source that reads only with credentials is
reported as a fact on the request — `GitSource.RequiresCredential` — the same

| --- | --- |
| URL, reads anonymously | `clone` (unchanged: pool-agent clones the URL) |
| HTTPS URL, `RequiresCredential` | `fetch` (§2) |
| Any other URL, `RequiresCredential` | `push` (§4) |

A `fetch`-delivered source parks in `awaiting_source` exactly as a
push-delivered one does, with the same bare pool-side origin (ADR 0058 §1). The
client then:

1. Obtains the credential with `git credential fill` for the URL's host, so

2. Calls a new endpoint,

The client reaches pool-agent only through the server, so the lent credential

This has been proposed before. ADR 0128 ("a private remote source is fetched with a credential the client lends") is almost exactly this, and ADR `26-10-10-545` rejected it. 545 §1 says "The pool never fetches from a remote and never holds a credential for one", and its rejected alternatives include both "the pool fetches with a credential the client lends" and "a credential callback". So building this means a new ADR that supersedes 545 §1, and it needs a reason that wasn't on the table then. 545's own Deferred section gives the natural one: the first create for a large repository moves the history twice (remote → client → pool), which is slow when the client's link is the slow one.

I think the idea is sound if it's shaped to avoid what sank 0128.

**1. Keep `delivery: cache` and change only how the cache gets filled.** Today the pin step (`cachedeliver.go` `deliverRemote`) returns what the pool is missing, and the client then fetches and pushes. Add one more step in between: the client asks the pool to fetch the missing commits itself.
- No new delivery enum.
- The per-remote cache, namespaces and sandbox clone stay as they are.
- Client fetch + push stays as the fallback.
- It helps local sources too: the pool fetches what's already published upstream, and the client pushes only unpushed commits and the dirty snapshot.

**2. "Pool tries, then asks the client" without a reverse channel.** 0128 rejected the callback because it needs a channel from the pool to one particular client, and a failed prompt ends up in the pool's reconcile loop instead of in front of the user. You can get the behaviour you want while keeping the client as the caller:

```
client → server → pool:  POST .../sources/{slug}/fetch            (no credential)
pool: git fetch anonymously (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, no helpers)
  ok   → 200, then client pins/completes as today
  auth → 401 {protocol, host, path}
client: "github.com/foo/bar needs credentials. Use your local git credentials? [Y/n]"
client: git credential fill  (protocol/host/path on stdin)
client → POST .../fetch {username, password}  (same request shape, retried)
  ok   → git credential approve      401 → git credential reject, ask again
```

The client already runs delivery in parallel with provisioning, while the user is still at the terminal, so the prompt shows up in the right place and nothing has to be persisted.

**3. Using git's credential framework.** It's `git credential fill` (with `approve`/`reject` afterwards). It runs the user's configured `credential.helper` chain: osxkeychain on macOS, Git Credential Manager on Windows, libsecret, or `gh auth setup-git`. If no helper has a credential it prompts on the terminal itself, so you get native behaviour for free. Send `path` as well, so users with `credential.useHttpPath` get per-repo credentials. On the pool side, pass the credential to git through the environment only, via a `GIT_ASKPASS` script or an inline `-c credential.helper=` that reads an env var. Never write it to the cache repo's config, and keep it out of server and pool request logs.

**4. SSH is the catch, and it's your own common case.** Credential helpers only cover HTTP(S). krpfz's upstream is `git@github.com:ibuildthecloud/discobox.git`, and SSH keys can't be lent safely: forwarding an agent lets the pool sign anything while it's connected. Two ways to handle it:
- Fall back to the current client fetch + push for SSH remotes, or
- For known forges (github.com and the like), rewrite the SSH URL to HTTPS for the pool's fetch and run `credential fill` against the HTTPS form. That works when the user has an HTTPS credential set up, such as a `gh` token; otherwise it falls back.

**5. Things the ADR has to answer:**
- **Credential exposure:** the credential passes through the server and the pool in memory. 0128 §3 argued this is "docker pull" trust, and that the pool proxy already sees cleartext secrets when it swaps sentinels.
- **Cache sharing:** a private repo fetched with user A's credential sits in a cache shared across the project. 545 §2/§7 already accepts project-level trust for pushed content, so this is consistent, but say so explicitly.
- **Reachability:** the pool now depends on the remote's speed and reachability, which 545 counted against the anonymous-fetch alternative. The client fallback makes that a performance risk rather than a correctness one.
- **Fetch scope:** the pool should fetch the checkout commit plus the remote's branches (the `refs/remotes/origin/*` that §6 needs), with `--filter` treated the same as the client's path.
- **Sandboxes as clients:** a discobox creating discoboxes would answer the 401 from its granted credential through the access protocol, not from `git credential fill`.

| Pool's pull result | Recorded on the source | What resolves it |
|---|---|---|
| Got the commit | (delivered) | nothing; the sandbox settles without a client |

| SSH remote, unreachable, or no remote | `missing_commit` (pool can't pull) | push only |

**"Push if we have it locally" in practice:**
- **Local source:** the client always has the commit, so it pushes. The pool's pull still helps: if it lands first, the push negotiates against what it fetched and only sends the unpushed commits and the snapshot. I'd let the pool pull and the client push run concurrently rather than make the client wait for the pull to fail.
- **Remote-URL source:** the client has the commit only if its `~/.cache/discobox/client/git` cache holds it. If it does, push; if not, offer the credential. The client never has to do a WAN fetch, which is exactly the double transfer this is meant to remove.

**What it gets you beyond speed:**
- **No client needed for public remotes:** 545's consequence "a remote-URL create needs a client until its source is delivered" goes away. Detached creates, creates from another box, or a future web UI just work.
- **Private remotes:** a private remote only needs a client when there's an auth failure, and then any client can answer it, for example a later `discobox attach` or `start`, not only the original `new`. That's worth deciding explicitly. Otherwise a detached create of a private repo just sits until the `awaiting_source` timeout.

**Things to pin down in the ADR:**
1. **Locking:** pool pull, client push and pins all write the same per-remote cache, so they need per-cache-key serialization for ref updates. The prune lock already gives you the hook for that.
2. **What the pool pulls:** the checkout commit plus the remote's branches into the cache's tracking refs, so §6's "reads as a clone of the remote" keeps working without the client supplying `refs/remotes/origin/*`.
3. **Classifying failures:** the pool has to tell auth failure from not-found from unreachable. GitHub answers a private repo with 401 over HTTPS, but "repository not found" for SSH. Only an HTTPS 401/403 should produce `needs_credential`.
4. **Supersession:** this supersedes 545 §1 ("the pool never fetches") and its rejection of "the pool fetches anonymously when the remote is public". # Architecture Decision Records

An ADR records a decision, the alternatives rejected, and why — at the time it
was made.

## When to write one

Only when either is true:

- A plausible alternative was rejected for a non-obvious reason.
- Something was deferred with a specific condition for revisiting it.

Otherwise skip the ADR and update the relevant `DESIGN.md`. Most changes do not
need one.

## Rules

- **Immutable.** Never edit an accepted ADR. Superseded by a new one that links
  back; mark the old one `Superseded by <id>`. An ADR's ID is as immutable as
  its text — never renumber one.
- **Outside the drill-down hierarchy.** ADRs live here, never next to code.
  `DESIGN.md`/`REVIEW.md` are read root-down by agents on every task; ADRs are
  not, and must not be, because they are history rather than current state.
- **Not a substitute for `DESIGN.md`.** When the work lands, update the live
  design docs to describe what now exists. The ADR keeps the "why we didn't";
  `DESIGN.md` keeps the "what is".

## Status lifecycle

`Proposed` → `Accepted` → (`Superseded by <id>`)

Use `Rejected` for decisions considered and declined; keep the file.

## Identifiers

An ADR's ID is `YY-MM-DD-RRR` — the date it was written, plus three random
decimal digits ([ADR 26-09-24-458](26-09-24-458-adr-ids-are-a-date-and-a-random-suffix.md)).
It is generated, never allocated from a sequence, so two branches in flight
cannot claim the same one.

```bash
python3 -c "import secrets; print(f'{secrets.randbelow(1000):03d}')"
```

- Filename `YY-MM-DD-RRR-<slug>.md`, heading `# YY-MM-DD-RRR — Title`, cited in
  prose and code comments as `ADR 26-09-24-458` or `ADR 26-09-24-458 §3`.
- The date is fixed when the file is created. Where it and the `Date` header
  disagree — an ADR written before a long review — the header is authoritative.
- If two branches somehow draw the same ID, **re-roll the suffix** on one of
  them. Nothing outside that branch cites it yet, and no value is the "correct"
  one to fight over.
- ADRs `0001`–`0149` predate this scheme and keep their four-digit numbers,
  which are cited across the tree. Both forms are permanent; the old ones sort
  first.

## Workflow

Nygard-style ADRs (see adr.github.io) combined with current-state design docs:

1. **Decide first.** Draft the ADR as `Proposed` and land it on its own,
   before implementation. Flipping it to `Accepted` is the decision gate —
   with review, the ADR's PR is where the review happens, and merge means
   accepted. Keep the status in the ADR header and the index table in sync.
2. **The accepted ADR is the spec** while implementation is in flight.
   `DESIGN.md` never describes in-progress or planned work — only what exists.
3. **DESIGN.md rides the code.** Each change that alters the architecture
   updates the affected `DESIGN.md` files in the same change, not as a
   follow-up pass. When the ADR's work fully lands, the live design docs
   describe the new state and the ADR keeps only the why.
4. **Plans are not documents.** Sequencing, checklists, and rollout order live
   in the task or branch driving the work; they are meant to go stale.
5. **Wrong decisions:** an `Accepted` ADR may still be amended while nothing
   has shipped against it. Once implementation has landed, supersede instead.

## Index

Both ID forms appear here, interleaved in the table's rough chronological
order: four-digit numbers up to `0149`, assigned before this scheme, and
`YY-MM-DD-RRR` since — plus the four earlier ADRs renumbered to resolve a
duplicated number.

# Open a PR and Drive It Green

Put the local commits on a GitHub branch, open a PR into `main`, and keep
working until the PR's head commit passes every check. The PR is where CI
proves the change; a human reviews and merges it.

Invoking this skill is authorization to push **one** branch to
`discobox-ai/discobox` (creating it on GitHub only — the local checkout stays on
its branch), open a PR from it, push further commits to it, edit the PR's body,
mark it ready, and comment on it. It is **not** authorization to merge, enable
auto-merge, push to `main`, force-push, request reviewers, or close anything —
ask for those.

## 0. Credentials

The repo is always `discobox-ai/discobox`; pass `--repo discobox-ai/discobox`
to every `gh` call. Outside a discobox, with `gh` logged in and a GitHub
remote, run the commands below directly and skip this section.

Inside a discobox there is no `gh` login. `origin` is the host checkout's own
remote — possibly a mirror — and `discobox` is the pool; in a discobox created
before ADR 26-10-10-545, `origin` is the pool and `upstream` is that remote.
Check `git remote -v`, and do not push to any of them by name: every GitHub call
goes through `discobox-access`, with the URL spelled out. `deliver-issue` and
`develop` ask for their own up front; check `discobox-access list` and
request only what is missing, in one request:

  "justification": "the user asked me to open a pull request for my local commits in discobox-ai/discobox and get its CI green",
  "uses": [

  "statements": [
    "allow read on anything in repository \"discobox-ai/discobox\"",
    "allow push on branch \"<branch>\" in repository \"discobox-ai/discobox\"",
    "allow create, update on pull request in repository \"discobox-ai/discobox\" when \"its head is <branch> and its base is main\"",
    "allow create on comment within pull request in repository \"discobox-ai/discobox\" when \"the pull request's head is <branch>\"",
    "allow rerun on workflow run in repository \"discobox-ai/discobox\" when \"it ran for branch <branch>\"",
    "deny force-push, delete on branch in anywhere",
    "deny merge, close on pull request in anywhere",
    "deny close, assign, retitle on issue in anywhere",
    "deny delete, update on label in anywhere",
    "deny delete on comment in anywhere",
    "deny cancel, delete on workflow run in anywhere",
    "deny dispatch on workflow in anywhere",
    "deny read on secret in anywhere"
  ],
  "definitions": {
    "repository": "a GitHub repository",
    "branch": "a git branch in a repository",
    "pull request": "a GitHub pull request",
    "issue": "a GitHub issue",
    "label": "a label a repository defines, which its issues and pull requests carry",

verbatim; leave it off when that is unset. End the body with whatever
attribution line the harness asks PR descriptions to end with.

## 3. Watch the checks

Everything below is about the PR's **head commit**, which must equal local
`HEAD`:

```bash
gh pr view <pr> --repo discobox-ai/discobox --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid
gh pr checks <pr> --repo discobox-ai/discobox --json name,state,bucket,link
```

Arm a Monitor that polls `gh pr checks` (one `discobox-access run` per poll,
every 60s) and exits when no check is in bucket `pending`, and keep working
while it runs. CI takes about seven minutes.

- **Green** — every check is `pass` or `skipping`, and CI's six jobs (`check`,
  `test`, `verify`, `build`, `darwin`, `windows`) are among them. Path-filtered
  workflows (`vm-image`, `vm-kernel`) appear only when their paths changed.
- **`cancel`** — CI cancels a PR's run when a newer push supersedes it. A
  cancelled check on an older commit is not a failure; one on the head commit
  is — re-list, then re-run it.
- **`fail`** — §4.

## 4. Fix, push, repeat

Read the failure: [ci-failures.md](ci-failures.md). Then:

1. Decide whether it is this change's. Failing on `main` too → pre-existing:
   note it on the PR, do not fix it here unless the user asks.
2. Reproduce it locally where you can (Windows- and macOS-only failures often
   reproduce with the tricks in ci-failures.md), fix the cause, and run the
   narrowest local check that covers it.
3. Run the fix through `discobox-review` — a CI fix is new code. The review's
   base has not moved, so only the files you edited need approval again.
4. If the fix changes behavior QA validated, run `test-fix` phase 2 again for
   the affected checks.
5. Commit conventionally, push the branch (fast-forward — never force), and go
   back to §3 against the new head.

After five failed rounds, stop and put the remaining failures to the user.

A conflict with `main` after the PR is open needs a rebase and a force-push:
ask first.

## Done when

The PR's head commit is local `HEAD`, every check on it is green, and the PR is
marked ready (`gh pr ready`). Do not merge.

Finish with: the PR URL, the head SHA, the green run IDs, and every CI failure
met on the way with its fix — or the pre-existing failures left for the user.

## Decision

### 1. Git comes from a client, always

Every Git source of a new sandbox is delivered by a client pushing it. Nothing
chooses between deliveries, on the server or anywhere else.

- **The pool never fetches from a remote and never holds a credential for
  one.** It receives pushes and serves fetches.
- **The server never runs Git.** It stays the byte proxy between a client and a
  pool that ADR 0058 §6 describes.
- **A sandbox's first clone is always from its pool.**

A client is whatever runs the CLI with the user's Git credentials: a person's
machine, or a discobox creating discoboxes with a credential it was granted
(ADR 26-09-24-630). A create that names a Git source and has no client parks in
`awaiting_source` and fails when that state times out (ADR 0001 §4). A
remote-URL source can be delivered by any client that can read the URL, not
only the one that created it.

### 2. A pool keeps one repository per remote

A pool holds a cache of bare repositories. Each source of each sandbox has a
Git namespace in one of them, `refs/namespaces/<sandboxID>-<slug>/`, in place
of a repository of its own. One object store per remote is what makes a push a
delta: the receiving side advertises what it already holds, from every
namespace, and the client sends the rest.

The cache is the pool's. It is not mounted into any sandbox and is not part of
any sandbox's tree. A namespace follows its sandbox: it is kept while the
sandbox is archived, removed when the control plane says the sandbox is gone,
and written out by an export (§9).

| The source | The cache key |
| --- | --- |
| Has a remote | the remote, normalized |
| Has none, and its client has a host identity | the source-data key, `originkey.Of(hostID, GitSource.Root())` |
| Neither | none: a cache of its own, removed with the sandbox |

- **A remote-URL source's remote is its URL. A local checkout's is reported by
  the client**: the remote its checked-out branch tracks, else `origin`, else
  its only remote. A branch that tracks nothing — how most work starts — must
  not move a checkout out of its remote's cache, so tracking is the first
  answer and not the only one; a branch that tracks a fork is in the fork's
  cache. A remote on a pool's origins host (ADR 26-10-08-561) is not a remote and
  is skipped: it is another sandbox's plumbing.
- **A remote is normalized** to host and path — lower-cased host, no scheme,
  user, default port, trailing slash or `.git` — so the HTTPS and SSH spellings
  of one repository share a cache.
- **The source-data key is the one that already names a source's pool
  storage** (`sourceDataKey`, `layout.SourceData`). It is not the sandbox's
  origin key (`SandboxOriginKey`), which names the primary source only and
  falls back to the host alone. It is empty without a host identity, which is
  the third row.
- **The scope is the pool.** A remote's cache is shared by every user of the
  project the pool belongs to, and the host identity is deliberately not part
  of a remote's key. Members of a project are trusted with each other's
  source, unpushed commits and dirty-workspace snapshots included. §7 bounds
  what a sandbox, which is not a member, can reach.
- **A cache is never shallow.** `receive.shallowUpdate` stays off: a
  repository's `shallow` file is the repository's, not a namespace's, and one
  shallow push would truncate every other sandbox's clone of that remote.

### 3. Delivery is a pin, or a fetch and a push, and it does not wait for the box

```mermaid
### 5. The cache remembers a remote; a namespace remembers a sandbox

- **A namespace holds what was delivered for one source of one sandbox** (§3),
  and nothing else writes it.
- **The cache holds the remote's own branches and tags**, as last delivered,
  under refs outside every namespace. That is what keeps a remote's history after
  its last sandbox is deleted, and what a client fetches in §3.
- **Everything else is unreachable once its sandbox is gone**, and `gc` prunes
  it.
- **The pool agent runs `git gc` on every cache on a schedule.** It is the
  pool's own periodic job, not a side effect of a push, so a cache that is
  only read is still repacked and pruned.
- **`gc` has a cache to itself.** Git's prune grace period runs from an
  object's age, and a pin or a delta push creates a ref at objects that may be
  old. So the pool agent holds a cache exclusively while it prunes, and a pin,
  a push or a namespace's removal waits. One repository per remote keeps that
  wait to the sandboxes of one remote.
- **A cache with no namespace that has gone unused for a retention period is
  removed whole.**

There is one repository per remote, not one object store for the pool. Each
is repacked, pruned, measured and removed on its own, and a damaged one costs
one remote's history.

### 6. A sandbox's remotes read as a clone of the real remote

The sandbox agent clones the source's namespace from the pool and then sets
the repository up as though it had cloned the source's remote:

| Remote | URL | Its remote-tracking refs come from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `origin` | the source's remote | the namespace's `refs/remotes/origin/*`, once, at materialization |
| `discobox` | the pool's origin route | the namespace's `refs/heads/*`, on every fetch |

Tags come with the clone. The checked-out branch tracks `origin/<branch>` when
the remote has that branch. A source with no remote has `discobox` alone, and
its branch tracks that.

- **The pool is never `origin` and the remote is never `upstream`.** The agent
  asserts the `discobox` remote's URL on every pass, as it asserts `origin`'s
  today; `origin` belongs to the sandbox after materialization, and moves when
  the sandbox fetches the real remote.
- **A sandbox sees new local commits only when a client pushes them.**
  `discobox push` and the attached client's push (ADR 26-09-05-008) update
  `discobox/<branch>`; whoever works in the sandbox fetches and rebases. The
  ref a sandbox's reported diff base follows (`UpstreamRef`, ADR 0058 §5) is
  therefore `refs/remotes/discobox/<branch>`, not `origin`'s.
- **A fetch from `origin` inside the sandbox goes to the real remote**, with
  the agent-credentials protocol where it is private (ADR 0031).

### 7. What a sandbox can reach is its own namespaces

Project trust (§2) is between people. A sandbox runs code nobody has read,
and the pool agent is what confines it. Hiding ids does not: a sandbox can
list the project's sandboxes and read the commit each was created at.

- **A sandbox's own route serves `git-upload-pack` only**, scoped to its
  source's namespace, on protocol v0. A v2 `upload-pack` serves any object
  asked for by id whatever namespace it is in — the reason ADR 0126's live
  origin is already pinned to v0 — and v0 refuses a want that no advertised
  ref reaches, but only while `uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant`,
  `allowReachableSHA1InWant`, `allowTipSHA1InWant` and `allowRefInWant` are
  off and `http.getanyfile` is false. The pool agent forces all five on the
  command line of every request it serves a sandbox, as it does for a live
  origin today, so nothing in a cache's own configuration can loosen them.
- **A sandbox never writes its own namespace.** Work leaves a sandbox through
  the worktree route, as now.
- **A discobox delivering to one it created** (ADR 26-09-24-630) is held to
  what it sent and what it already has. The pool agent accepts a ref from it
  only when every object the ref reaches arrived in that push or is reachable
  from the calling sandbox's own namespaces, and it pins only at a commit
  those namespaces reach. Git itself accepts a ref at any object the store
  holds, sent or not, so this is the pool agent's check and not Git's. The
  caller is told what its own namespaces hold and nothing more, which still
  makes a child cut from its own checkout a delta.
- **The cache a sandbox caller names is its own claim** — the remote and the
  host identity are its word. The check above is why that is harmless: naming
  another cache gives it nothing there it did not send.
- **Fetching a cache's remote tips (§3) is a project member's**, never a
  sandbox's. A discobox creating from a remote URL fetches from the remote
  alone.

### 8. Existing sandboxes are left as they are

Nothing that exists is rewritten, in a sandbox or on a pool.

### 3. Delivery is a pin, or a fetch and a push, and it does not wait for the box

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Remote
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Pool cache
    participant S as Sandbox
    C->>R: ls-remote (pin the commit)
    C->>P: create, then "deliver commit X"
    alt pool holds X
        P-->>C: pinned
    else pool lacks X
        C->>P: fetch what the pool has (remote-URL source only)
        C->>R: fetch the rest
        C->>P: push the rest
    end
    P-->>S: origin has the pin
    S->>P: clone
```

1. **Pin.** The client names every ref of the delivery (the table below) and
   the object each points at; for a remote URL, `ls-remote` gives it all of
   them. The pool creates each ref whose object its cache already holds,
   reachable from a ref. When that is all of them, nothing is transferred. An
   object that is present but unreachable is not pinned.
2. **Otherwise the client supplies what the pin could not.** From a local
   checkout it already holds the objects and pushes. For a remote URL it keeps a bare repository per
   remote in its own cache directory, fetches into it from the pool and then
   from the remote, and pushes; the second fetch is negotiated against the
   first, so each leg carries only what the next host lacks.
3. **The push starts when the create returns.** The route is addressed by
   sandbox and slug as today (0058 §3). The server names the cache and the
   namespace when it forwards, so the pool needs no record of the sandbox and
   no container to accept it. The push, and the fetch that feeds it, run while
   the image is pulled and the sandbox boots; a pool that is not up yet is the
   only thing they wait for. A sandbox whose source has landed by the time its
   agent answers never parks.

The first create for a remote that neither the client nor the pool has seen
moves the full history twice, remote to client to pool. That is the price of
§1, and it is paid once per remote per pool.

What is delivered, into the source's namespace:

| Refs | Hold |
| --- | --- |
| `refs/heads/*` | what the sandbox starts from, as today: the source's branch, or the conventional branch a tag or bare commit is pushed to; and what `discobox push` adds later |
| the snapshot ref | a dirty workspace (ADR 0001); a directory with no repository (ADR 0045) is delivered as it is today |
| `refs/remotes/origin/*`, `refs/tags/*` | the remote's branches and tags as the client knows them: all of them for a remote-URL source, the checkout's remote-tracking refs and tags for a local one |

The last row is what lets a sandbox read as a clone of the remote (§6)
without reaching it: a remote-URL sandbox has every branch and tag, as it does
today, and a local checkout's `origin/<branch>` is where the remote was, not
where the developer's unpushed commits are.

**A shallow checkout is refused by the client**, with the reason and `git
fetch --unshallow`. It cannot be pushed into a cache (§2), and deepening
someone's checkout is not the CLI's to do.

### 4. Every source of a sandbox is delivered this way

A sandbox's sources are its primary, each `--include`, and each source its
primary declares in `.discobox/sources.json` (ADR 0056). Each is its own
source with its own cache key (§2) and its own namespace, pinned or pushed as
§3 says, all at once. Nothing distinguishes how they travel.

ADR 0056 stands — a local checkout beside the primary wins, a fallback lands
where that checkout would have, explicit beats declared, no recursion — with
one change: **a remote primary declares sources too.** 0056 refused it because
reading the file meant cloning on the client. It does not: the client reads
the one file from the remote at the pinned commit.

The sources of a create are fixed in the create request, so the file is read
before the create, and reading it must not wait on the history. The client
fetches the pinned commit alone, with no trees or blobs (`--depth=1
--filter=tree:0`), into a throwaway repository and reads the file from there,
which fetches the few objects on its path. Tried against
`discobox-ai/discobox` on GitHub while this was written, that took about a
second and 100 KiB. The throwaway repository is not the client's cache of the
remote, which stays complete. A remote that refuses a filtered fetch gets the
commit at depth 1 instead.

# 26-10-23-948 — A pool pulls a cached source first, and a client supplies what the pull could not

- **Status**: Proposed
- **Date**: 2026-10-23
- **Supersedes**, once accepted and for sandboxes created after it:
  [26-10-10-545](26-10-10-545-git-reaches-a-pool-only-from-a-client-and-is-cached-there-per-remote.md)
  §1's "the pool never fetches from a remote and never holds a credential for
  one" and "a create that names a Git source and has no client parks", §3's
  order of delivery for a remote-URL source, and its rejection of "the pool
  fetches with a credential the client lends" and "the pool fetches
  anonymously when the remote is public".
- **Relates to**:
  [0128](0128-a-private-remote-source-is-fetched-with-a-credential-the-client-lends.md)
  (rejected; §8 here takes up its lending mechanics, not its choice of
  delivery),
  [26-09-24-005](26-09-24-005-attaching-to-a-discobox-awaiting-its-source-delivers-it.md),
  [26-09-24-630](26-09-24-630-a-discobox-delivers-the-source-of-the-discoboxes-it-creates.md),
  [0031](0031-agent-credentials-are-a-portable-protocol-with-ephemeral-sentinels.md).

## Context

ADR 26-10-10-545 delivers every source by a client: the client pins what the
pool's per-remote cache already holds and pushes the rest, and for a
remote-URL source it first fetches the rest from the remote into its own
cache. The pool never fetches. That bought one delivery path, no credential
anywhere but the client, and a cache that makes every create after the first
a delta.

It left three costs, two of them named in its own Consequences and Deferred:

- **The first create for a remote moves its history twice**, remote to client
  to pool, through the client's link. 545 deferred streaming the pack through
  the client "when the first create for a large repository is what people
  wait on". A pool usually sits on a better link to a forge than a laptop
  does, and a pool fetch moves the history once.
- **A remote-URL create needs a client until its source is delivered.** A
  public repository cannot be started detached, from another box without its
  own fetch, or from anything that is not the CLI — although nothing about it
  needs a credential.
- **A sandbox client moves the history through its own proxy.** A discobox
  creating discoboxes from a remote URL fetches into its sandbox and pushes
  back to the pool it runs on.

545 rejected the pool fetching anonymously because it "is a second delivery
chosen by probing a remote", and rejected lending a credential (ADR 0128)
because "a user's credential transits the server and the pool, and a create
becomes a credential-bearing request". This ADR keeps one delivery and no
probe-time choice: the cache delivery stays `cache`, the pool's pull is one
more way the cache is filled before a client is asked, and a client supplies
whatever the pull could not — by the push it already has, or by lending a
credential for one request it makes itself. The create is never
credential-bearing; the credential travels only in a request a client makes
in answer to a recorded failure, while a person is there to answer it.

## Decision

### 1. Delivery stays `cache`; the pool pulls first

`GitSource.Delivery` keeps the one value 545 gave it. Nothing new is chosen at
create, and the server still refuses a create that names a delivery.

For every source whose cache key is a remote (545 §2), **the pool agent pulls
that remote into the source's cache when it is asked to create the sandbox**,
anonymously, before and alongside anything a client sends:

- It fetches the remote's branches and tags into the cache's refs outside
  every namespace (545 §5), and the source's checkout commit if no branch or
  tag reaches it.
- If the cache then holds the checkout commit, **the pool pins the
  namespace itself** with the refs 545 §3's table names — the branch at the
  commit, `refs/remotes/origin/*` and `refs/tags/*` from what it fetched —
  and the source is delivered. No client is involved.
- A source with no remote (545 §2's second and third rows) is not pulled. A
  client delivers it as today.

The pull runs as Git, with no credential helper, no terminal prompt
(`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`) and no SSH agent, bounded by a stall timeout. It
writes refs outside every namespace and a namespace's refs only when it pins,
so it needs nothing from a concurrent client push but object writes Git
already makes safe. `gc` keeps its exclusive hold (545 §5); a pull waits for
it like a pin.

### 2. The pool pulls over HTTPS

The pull's URL is the source's remote when that is an HTTPS URL, and
otherwise **`https://` plus the remote's normalized cache key** (545 §2's
host and path). An SSH remote such as `git@github.com:owner/repo.git` is
pulled from `https://github.com/owner/repo`. A host with no HTTPS Git
service fails the pull as unreachable (§3), and a client pushes.

The HTTPS spelling is what a credential is filled for (§5): Git's credential
helpers answer HTTP only, and a lent SSH key or a forwarded agent would let
the pool sign as the user for as long as it held it.

### 3. A pull that falls short is recorded, per source, with what would fix it

The pool reports each pulled source's result to the control plane in its
create answer, and the server records it on the source's delivery state:

| The pull | Recorded | What a client may do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Holds the commit, and pinned | delivered | nothing |
| Refused for authentication (HTTP 401, or 403 with a Git auth challenge) | `needs_credential`, with the `protocol`, `host` and `path` of the URL asked | push, or lend a credential (§5) |
| Reached the remote, which does not have the commit | `missing_commit` | push |
| Could not reach a Git service, or stalled | `unreachable` | push |

The sandbox stays in `awaiting_source` while any source is owed, as it does
today. **Delivery is recorded per source**: the sandbox resumes once every
source is delivered, whether the pool pinned it or a client completed it, and
`SourceDeliveredAt` records the last of them. A client's
`complete-source-push` names only the sources it delivered; the server
refuses one that names a source already delivered at another commit, and
accepts one that repeats a delivery at the same commit.

### 4. A client pushes what it holds, and lends a credential only when it does not

A client waits on the recorded result of each source it may deliver, except
that **a client that already holds a source's checkout commit pushes it
without waiting**. Pushing is preferred whenever the client has the commit:
it needs no credential to leave the client and no remote to be reachable,
and 545 §3's negotiation sends only what the cache — including whatever the
pull has landed — still lacks.

| The source | The client |
| --- | --- |
| A local checkout | holds the commit: pins and pushes as 545 §3 says, at once |
| A remote URL whose commit is in the client's cache of that remote | pushes from that cache, at once |
| A remote URL the client does not hold, pull delivered | nothing |
| …recorded `needs_credential` | lends a credential (§5) if its user agrees; otherwise fetches and pushes as 545 §3 says |
| …recorded `missing_commit` or `unreachable` | fetches and pushes as 545 §3 says; if the remote does not have the commit there either, the create fails with that reason |

A local checkout's unpushed commits and dirty snapshot exist only on the
client, so a local source always needs its client; what the pull adds there
is the remote's published history, which shrinks the push.

**Any client may answer**, not only the creating one: a later `discobox
attach` or `start` of a sandbox awaiting its source delivers it
(ADR 26-09-24-005), and now that includes answering `needs_credential`. A
detached create of a private repository waits for one, and fails when
`awaiting_source` times out, as an undelivered source does today.

### 5. A credential is lent in a request the client makes, for that request

Lending takes up ADR 0128 §2's mechanics:

1. The client asks Git for a credential: `git credential fill` with the
   recorded `protocol`, `host` and `path`, so whatever supplies the user's Git
   over HTTPS — a keychain, Git Credential Manager, `gh auth setup-git`,
   libsecret, a store — supplies this, and a helper keyed by path
   (`credential.useHttpPath`) gets the path. With no helper that answers, Git
   prompts on the terminal itself.
2. It calls `POST .../sandboxes/{s}/sources/{slug}/pull` with the username and
   password. The server forwards the request to the pool agent, which pulls
   as §1 says **inside that request**, with the credential reaching Git only
   through the process environment (a `GIT_ASKPASS` helper reading an
   inherited variable). It is never written to the cache's configuration, a
   credential store, a resource, an event or a log, on the server or the
   pool, and neither keeps it after the request returns.
3. An authentication failure answers 401; the client runs `git credential
   reject` and asks again while its user is there. A pull that pins answers
   with the delivery, and the client runs `git credential approve`.

**A credential is lent only with its user's consent.** An interactive client
asks before running `fill` — "github.com/owner/repo needs credentials to
pull on the pool. Use your Git credentials? [Y/n]" — and a non-interactive one
lends only when told to by a flag or a configuration setting; otherwise it
fetches and pushes, and nothing leaves the client.

**A sandbox never lends.** A discobox creating discoboxes holds sentinels, not
credentials (ADR 0031), and a sentinel is worthless outside its proxy. It
fetches and pushes as 545 §3 says, through its own proxy.

### 6. What a pull may reach is what the create named

The pool pulls only the remote the source's cache key names, and only into
that cache. A sandbox caller's create names its own remote (545 §7), so a
sandbox can make its pool pull any public HTTPS repository into the cache
for that repository's key — what it could already do by pushing the same
history, with the bytes moving once instead of through its proxy. 545 §7's
check on a sandbox's pins and pushes is unchanged: the pool's own pin for a
sandbox caller's source is made only from what the pull fetched for it.

A pool's pull goes out from the pool host, as its proxy's traffic does; a
pool whose host cannot reach a forge records `unreachable` and its clients
push.

## Alternatives rejected

- **Probe at create and choose a delivery (ADR 0128 §1).** The client would
  report whether the remote reads anonymously and the server would choose
  `clone`, `fetch` or `push`. It brings back the choice 545 removed, and the
  client's probe says nothing about the pool's reach. Here the pull is always
  tried and its recorded result is the probe.
- **The pool asks a client for a credential through a callback during the
  pull.** It needs a channel from the pool to one particular client, which
  0128 and 545 both rejected, and a prompt that fails lands in the pool's
  reconcile. Recording the failure and having a client answer it in its own
  request gets the same "pull first, credential on demand" behaviour with no
  reverse channel.
- **Lend the credential with the create.** A create is persisted and
  reconciled asynchronously, so the credential would be stored until the pool
  reached it (0128's own rejection).
- **Prefer lending over pushing when the client holds the commit.** It would
  move the history once from the forge, but it sends a credential through the
  server and pool when no credential is needed: the push negotiates against
  what the pull already landed, and costs only what the cache lacks.
- **Have the client wait for the pull before pushing a local source.** A
  local source always needs its client for unpushed work, and an anonymous
  pull of a private remote is a guaranteed failure; waiting would make every
  local create of a private repository slower by that round trip.
- **Pull over SSH with a lent key or a forwarded agent.** A key or agent on
  the pool can sign anything for as long as it is held; HTTPS credentials are
  scoped by the forge and filled by Git for one URL.
- **Pull with a project secret the proxy swaps in.** The server would own a
  user's Git credential, usable by every later create on the pool — the
  opposite of lending (0128's rejection, unchanged).

## Consequences

- A create from a public HTTPS-reachable remote needs no client: it can run
  detached, from a box that does not fetch it first, or from a non-CLI
  caller. 545's "a remote-URL create needs a client until its source is
  delivered" holds only for private remotes and local sources.
- The first create for a remote the client does not hold moves the history
  once, forge to pool, when the pull or a lent credential succeeds.
- A private HTTPS remote can be delivered with a credential that transits the
  server and the pool in memory, for one request, with the user's consent.
  That is new exposure on the control plane, bounded by the request, and the
  pull route is the one server route whose body carries a credential.
- The pool depends on a remote's speed and reachability again, but only for
  speed: a pull that fails or stalls is a recorded result a client answers by
  pushing.
- A private repository pulled with one member's credential is in a cache
  every member of the project shares, as one member's push already is
  (545 §2).
- Delivery is recorded per source, and `complete-source-push` covers only the
  sources a client delivered. The sandboxes `DESIGN.md`'s "completion is one
  report for the whole sandbox" changes with it.
- The pool agent gains a pull and a self-pin path, and its create answer
  carries each source's pull result; the CLI gains the credential prompt, the
  pull request, and a wait on recorded results for remote-URL sources.

## Deferred

- **Pulling for a source whose cache key is a client directory.** It has no
  remote to pull. Revisit if local sources without a remote become common.
- **Refreshing a cache's remote refs on a schedule**, so a later create finds
  the remote's newest commits already there. Revisit when creates from a
  remote routinely miss on commits the pool's last pull predates.
- **A non-HTTPS pull** (a host with SSH-only Git, `git://`). Revisit if such a
  host is a project's primary remote.

**What it decides:**
- **Pool pulls first:** delivery stays `cache`, so there's no new mode. When the pool agent is asked to create the sandbox, it pulls the source's remote anonymously. If that gets the checkout commit, the pool sets up the sandbox's copy itself and no client is needed.
- **SSH remotes are pulled over HTTPS:** for example, `git@github.com:owner/repo.git` is pulled from `https://github.com/owner/repo`. That's what lets git's credential helpers apply, since they only cover HTTPS.
- **Failures are recorded per source:** `needs_credential` (with the host and path to ask about), `missing_commit`, or `unreachable`. The sandbox waits until every source is delivered, whether the pool or a client delivered it.
- **Push is preferred:** if the client already has the commit (always true for a local checkout), it pushes right away without waiting for the pull. Otherwise, on `needs_credential` it offers to lend a credential; failing that, it fetches and pushes as it does today.
- **Lending a credential:** the CLI asks the user first, then runs `git credential fill`, so the macOS keychain, Git Credential Manager or `gh` supply it. It sends the credential in a one-off pull request it makes itself, and nothing on the server or pool keeps it. A 401 leads to `credential reject` and another prompt. A non-interactive client lends only when a flag or setting allows it, and a sandbox never lends.
- **Any client can answer:** a later `attach` or `start` can supply the credential, not just the original `new`.
